1.pericope_label: Jesus departs from the temple; the disciples point out its buildings, and he foretells that not one stone shall be left upon another

schools.summary: Gill has Christ take his final leave and begin in the leaving to fulfil the desolation he had foretold; Calvin reads the disciples pointing at the buildings as unbelief rather than admiration, their eyes so dazzled by the present splendour that they could scarcely hope the kingdom of Christ would arise, and gives the reason behind the sentence, that God determined by this dreadful example to take vengeance on the nation for rejecting his Son.

Henry presses the wording, that Christ did not merely go out of the temple but departed from it, never to return, so that the house Christ leaves is left desolate indeed; he has Christ depart only when driven away, keeps the twelve with him as the seed of the gospel church, and holds that while sacrifice was tied to the temple door, prayer and praise and preaching are as acceptable in one place as another.

Clarke shows from the word that answered refers to nothing said and no question asked, notes that the negative is absent from several excellent manuscripts so that the clause reads simply consider all these things, and places the last words at the moment of leaving; Wesley carries the ploughing of the temple site after the burning.

Ellicott prefers the reading of the best manuscripts, fills in the great stones and gates and porticos and the offerings of forty-six years, and reports from Josephus that Titus left only two or three towers standing while modern excavation reaches no further than the substructures; Barnes insists how improbable the thing was when spoken and rests the proof on a Jewish priest who would have said nothing to confirm the prophecies of Jesus; Robertson dates the end of the public teaching and calls it a tragic moment; Lightfoot quotes the rabbinic saying that a man who never saw Herod Temple never saw a fine building, and dates the ploughing to the ninth of Ab.

debates.question: Why did the disciples point out the buildings?

sides.position: they were pleased with what they showed him, having lived in Galilee and seldom seen a structure reckoned among the wonders of the world
the sight was meant to make him recall his words of evil omen, which is a far more natural account than the alternative
it was unbelief: dazzled by the present splendour they could scarcely hope the kingdom of Christ would arise

debates.question: How was the prediction fulfilled?

sides.position: Titus ordered city and temple dug up, leaving two or three towers, so visitors could hardly believe the place inhabited
exactly within forty years, on the testimony of a Jewish priest whose history reads like a running commentary on the prophecy
the foundations were dug up after the burning and the ground then ploughed, on the ninth of Ab

outliers: Robertson alone marks that the public teaching ends here, calling it a tragic moment.
Lightfoot alone supplies the rabbinic anecdote of walls built winding like waves to take plaster, which the Rabbins begged might be left as it was.
themes: a departure that is itself a sentence
stones admired and stones counted
a prophecy checked against a hostile historian
a house left desolate when Christ leaves it

3.pericope_label: On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask privately when these things shall be, and what shall be the sign of his coming and of the end of the world

schools.summary: Gill places the mount east of the city and over against the temple and explains why the view was open, the eastern wall being built lower so that the high priest might see the temple gate from it; Calvin explains how the confusion arose, that believing from infancy the temple would stand till the end of time they could not suppose the kingdom would come while the building stood, and so flew at once to a triumph.

Clarke counts three questions but reports the contrary view that they are parts of one, reads the phrase as the close of an economy, and supports the rendering from Aristotle; Wesley says flatly that they inquired confusedly, as though temple and consummation were one thing, and allots the verses of the chapter to each question in turn.

Barnes counts three questions and says the reply intermingles the two subjects so that it is sometimes hard to tell which a remark belongs to; Ellicott marks the first occurrence of the term for the coming and explains what this age and the age to come meant in the common speech of the day; Robertson adds that the same word is used in the papyri for the visit of an emperor, grants the discourse the most difficult problem in the Synoptic Gospels, and refuses to say whether the disciples thought the events simultaneous; Lightfoot approaches from what the nation expected of the Messiah days, drawn out of the Babylonian Sanhedrin.

debates.question: How many questions were asked, and did the askers know what they asked?

sides.position: three questions, answered by intermingling the two subjects, both being describable in the same words
three, though some make them parts of one question answered only of the Jewish state
they inquired confusedly, as though the fall of the temple and the end of the world were one thing, while the Lord answered distinctly
there is no way to tell whether they supposed the events simultaneous

debates.question: What does the end of the world mean here?

sides.position: the end of the age, that is of an economy, an accommodated use of a word whose proper force is eternal
the end of the age in the common speech of the day, this age being the time up to the Messiah and the age to come the era he would inaugurate

outliers: Gill alone explains the open view from the lower eastern wall and the burning of the red heifer on that mount.
Lightfoot alone reconstructs the apostles meaning from the tradition of the school of Elias about the righteous raised from the dead.
themes: a question asked in private
three questions or one
a term that would later fill the Epistles
expectations learned in childhood

4.pericope_label: Take heed that no man deceive you: false Christs, wars and rumours of wars, famines and earthquakes, which are the beginning of sorrows

schools.summary: Gill reads the answer as given not to indulge curiosity but to caution them against deceivers; Calvin opens from the disciples disappointment, that they looked for a triumph and got an exhortation to long patience, as if told they wished to seize the prize at the outset with the course still to run, and narrows the first sign to the one class of error that introduced every later one.

Henry sets the terms of the whole discourse, that Christ answers the question about signs and not the question about times, and holds that the prophecy primarily respects the destruction of Jerusalem while under that type looking as far as the general judgment.

Clarke numbers the signs and supplies the instances of desert pretenders from Josephus, calling it a just judgment that a people who rejected the true Christ should be delivered to false ones; Wesley numbers the first sign the same way.

Barnes says there is abundant evidence the first sign was fulfilled, notes that the empire was at peace when the words were spoken and that four emperors afterwards died violently within eighteen months, and distinguishes rumours of wars from wars; Ellicott dissents that no direct fulfilment of the false Christs is recorded, reads the tense as a double future, and confines the wars chiefly to those affecting the Jews; Robertson takes the verb in its causative force and turns the clause into counsel not to be terrified out of one wits; Lightfoot adds the shaking of the empire itself and the burning of the Capitol.

debates.question: Was the prediction of false Christs fulfilled before the fall of Jerusalem?

sides.position: yes, abundantly; Josephus supplies the instances, including an Egyptian who led thirty thousand into the desert
no direct fulfilment is recorded either in the New Testament or by Josephus, and the figure usually named appeared long after the city fell

debates.question: What does the prophecy primarily respect?

sides.position: what lay near at hand, the destruction of Jerusalem and the setting up of Christ kingdom, while under that type looking as far as the general judgment
the commotions in Judea only at this stage, since the flame is said later to spread wider

outliers: Robertson alone remarks that our word planet comes from the root of the verb for leading astray.
Ellicott alone notes how aptly the historian titled his second book for this part of the prophecy.
themes: a question about times refused
deceivers who come in the name they usurp
peace at the moment of the prediction
pangs that are only the beginning

9.pericope_label: They shall deliver you up to be afflicted and ye shall be hated of all nations; many shall be offended and shall betray and hate one another

schools.summary: Gill marks the reversal, that men looking for a temporal kingdom are promised affliction and death, and describes the professors who stumbled at the cross once they saw apostles beaten and killed; Calvin treats the hatred as a distinct trial added to ordinary affliction, painful because the children of God are not distinguished from the despisers of God, and calls the offence from bad examples the most violent temptation of all.

Clarke personifies the affliction, so that they are delivered into its own hand to be harassed by every mode of inventive torture, and supplies the Roman annalist on the persecution under Nero, where those first seized betrayed a great multitude; Wesley puts the sting in the pretext, that they were delivered up as if they were themselves the cause of these evils, and notes they would be hated even by those who tolerate every other sect.

Barnes documents the fulfilment from the Acts and makes the betraying a matter of securing one own safety by revealing names and hiding-places; Ellicott makes the adverb point to synchronism rather than sequence, narrows the hatred to the heathen nations, and finds the mutual hatred fulfilled in the faction-fights at Jerusalem and the bitterness of the Judaisers against Paul; Robertson reads the periphrastic future as a continuous process and observes that the most glorious name in the world today was soon to be a byword of shame; Lightfoot connects the apostolic word that judgment must begin at the house of God.

debates.question: Who are the all nations that will hate them?

sides.position: both Jew and Gentile, though the phrase may mean the Gentiles in particular since the parallels name the Jewish persecution separately
the heathen nations, as when the sect was everywhere spoken against at Rome
even those who tolerate every other sect, since in no nation will the children of the devil tolerate the children of God

debates.question: Who are the many that shall be offended?

sides.position: professors who were advocates while things were quiet and stumbled at the cross when persecution came
believers who found a stumbling-block in the new aspects of truth, the slowness of the victory, or the delay of the coming

outliers: Robertson alone turns the clause into an honour, that the disciples would count it a distinction to be dishonoured for the Name.
Clarke alone supplies the Roman annalist on how the first confessions betrayed a multitude.
themes: a kingdom expected and a scourging given
a name that became a byword
betrayal as a bid for safety
love cooling where offences abound

11.pericope_label: Many false prophets shall rise and deceive many; because iniquity shall abound the love of many shall wax cold, but the gospel shall be preached in all the world

schools.summary: Gill allows every candidate at once for the abounding iniquity, the malice of persecutors, the treachery of apostates, the errors of false teachers and the plain wickedness of lives, and makes the endurance a perseverance in faith, doctrine and holiness; Calvin distinguishes these false teachers from the earlier impostors as a standing danger in every age, turns the cooling of love on the reader by observing that the clearer the gospel shows men malice the more even good minds lose the desire to do good, and reads the promise of a world-wide preaching as given to raise minds that were cast down.

Clarke takes the end as the destruction of the Jewish polity and the salvation as deliverance, adding that not a single Christian perished when Jerusalem fell; Wesley says the preaching was not universal, this not being done yet, but general through the several parts of the world and accomplished before the city fell.

Barnes narrows the false prophets to men appearing during the siege, quoting Josephus that the zealots suborned them to keep the people from deserting, and glosses the verb for cooling as an old word no longer used in this sense outside the Bible; Ellicott prefers lawlessness as the rendering and says no word could better describe Judea then, and insists the words about all the world must not be strained beyond what the hearers would understand, namely the Roman empire; Robertson agrees the language should not be pressed too literally; Lightfoot gives the reason for the order, that Jerusalem was not to be destroyed before the gospel had spread, so that the world might have an undeniable testimony in the vengeance poured out on that city.

debates.question: Who are the false prophets of this verse?

sides.position: teachers in every age who corrupt sound doctrine, the Church under the gospel being no less exposed than under the Law
prophets appearing during the siege itself, suborned by the zealots to promise aid from heaven
named heretical teachers who pretended to a spirit of prophecy and new revelations

debates.question: What is the end that must be endured to?

sides.position: the destruction of the Jewish polity, the salvation being deliverance from it
more probably the close of life and final salvation
both at once, since endurance to the end of life is always the condition of salvation while the context points to the close of this period

outliers: Calvin alone turns the cooling of love into a charge against the reader, that kindness comes to seem thrown away because experience shows almost all ungrateful.
Lightfoot alone explains the order of events, that the gospel had to spread first so that the vengeance might be an undeniable testimony.
themes: a danger that outlasts its first instance
lawlessness as the plain name for the time
a love that cools without being lost
a world that must hear before a city falls

15.pericope_label: When ye see the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel standing in the holy place, let him that readeth understand

schools.summary: Gill clears away the wrong candidates rather than naming the right one, refusing a Roman statue, the golden eagle of Herod, the image of Tiberius and the statue of Adrian in turn; Calvin supplies the reason the prophet is cited at all, that the overthrow was incredible and it seemed strange the disciples could not be saved without being torn from the nation to which the covenants had been committed, so that they must not be too strongly attached to a temple God had limited to a fixed time.

Clarke and Wesley both make the abomination the Roman army and explain the name by the ensigns, Clarke adding the report that the Romans brought their ensigns into the temple and sacrificed to them by the eastern gate, Wesley widening the holy place to the whole city and the very mount where the discourse was given.

Barnes calls the phrase a Hebrew expression for an abominable destroyer and notes the second evangelist says simply standing where it ought not; Ellicott alone refuses the consensus, since the warning precedes the destruction and the thing stands in the Holy Place, and looks instead to the faction-fights and profanations within the city; Robertson derives the noun from a verb for feeling nausea at a stench and recalls the altar to Zeus set on the altar of Jehovah; Lightfoot renders the Daniel verse himself and holds the parenthesis spoken for the certainty of the prophecy rather than its obscurity.

debates.question: What is the abomination of desolation?

sides.position: the Roman army, named an abomination for the images and eagles carried before the legions
not the troops or the eagles at all, since the warning precedes the destruction and the thing stands in the Holy Place; rather the faction-fights and profanations within the city
none of the statues commonly proposed, whether Herod golden eagle, the image of Tiberius or the statue of Adrian

debates.question: Why the aside to the reader?

sides.position: not for the obscurity of the prophecy but for its certainty, that a siege means certain destruction
it stands in the second gospel too, and was probably not spoken by Jesus himself

outliers: Ellicott alone breaks with every other voice on the identification, and gives two reasons of chronology and place.
Calvin alone uses the verse to loosen the disciples attachment to the temple rather than to date the siege.
themes: a prophecy quoted to make the incredible credible
an army that is itself an idol
a holy place as wide as a city
a reader told to understand

16.pericope_label: Then let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains; let not him on the housetop or in the field return back for anything

schools.summary: Gill reads the direction as telling those in the city and in the towns alike not to shelter in Jerusalem on the strength of its fortifications, and has the man in the field at the plough or the sowing; Calvin draws the inference that once the temple was profaned the services of the Law would soon be abolished, so that nothing would be more desirable than distance from the place, the calamities coming too suddenly to leave time for the most rapid flight.

Clarke says the counsel was remembered and wisely followed, cites the early historians that the believers left for Pella and other places beyond Jordan so that not one perished, and gives the reason the warning is absolute, that once the army sat down before the city there would be no further escape; Wesley supplies the detail that made the signal legible, the unexpected withdrawal of the Romans after their first advance.

Barnes explains why the mountains, the hills of Palestine abounding in caves which were in every age the refuge of men pursued, and draws the moral that the man on the roof should not stop even for a garment; Ellicott dates the flight and names the town on the northern boundary beyond Jordan, corrects the plural clothes to a singular cloak, and explains the continuous terrace of flat roofs ending at the gates; Robertson gives the rabbinic name for that route, the road of the roofs.

debates.question: Was the warning obeyed?

sides.position: yes; the believers left for Pella and places beyond Jordan, and not one of them perished
yes, and the signal was the unexpected withdrawal of the Romans after their first advance

debates.question: Why such haste over a garment?

sides.position: the delay itself would endanger life
the labourer worked in a short tunic and left the outer garment at home in the city, so going back meant going back into danger
once the army encamped there would be no possibility of escape at all

outliers: Robertson alone gives the rabbinic name for the route across the roofs.
Barnes alone explains the choice of the mountains from the caves that had always sheltered the pursued.
themes: a city refused as a refuge
a road across the rooftops
a cloak not worth returning for
a warning that was actually taken

19.pericope_label: Woe to them that are with child; pray that your flight be not in winter nor on the sabbath; great tribulation such as was not since the beginning, and the days shortened for the elect

schools.summary: Gill insists it is no crime nor judgment to be with child and lists what makes winter flight hard; Calvin looks past the physical to the most destructive plague of all, that the light of heavenly doctrine was extinguished among them, and sets the shortening beside the prophet small seed without which the people would have been as Sodom.

Clarke says no history can furnish a parallel, with rapine and famine within and fire and sword without, observes that our Lord wept at the foresight, puts the number who perished at eleven hundred thousand, and reports the rabbinic observation about the first temple falling in summer; Wesley adds that the Jews thought it unlawful to walk above two thousand paces on the sabbath and that in the event the flight fell in the spring.

Barnes draws out the logic of praying about a calamity that cannot be prevented, and takes the content of the tribulation from the third evangelist; Ellicott prefers alas for them to woe unto them and calls the tone pity rather than denunciation, explains that rules were given for what lay in their power while what lay outside it might be prayed about, and traces the superlative to Daniel; Robertson treats the past tense of the shortening as a prophetic figure, the future regarded as past; Lightfoot finds a symmetry, that God lengthened the time for the elect before the destruction and shortened it for their sake in it.

debates.question: For whose sake were the days shortened?

sides.position: the elect are the Christians, and without the shortening the whole nation would have been destroyed
God lengthened the time for the elect before the destruction and shortened it for their sake within it

debates.question: Why pray about a calamity already decreed?

sides.position: because the circumstances may be mitigated, as we rightly pray that known calamities come mildly
because rules were given for what lay within their power, while what lay outside their will might lawfully be prayed about

outliers: Ellicott alone insists the tone of the woe is pity rather than denunciation.
Calvin alone ranks the extinguishing of heavenly doctrine above the slaughter as the worst plague of the siege.
themes: a burden that cannot run
a season and a day prayed about
a siege without parallel in history
days cut short for a remnant

23.pericope_label: If any say lo here is Christ, believe it not; false Christs and false prophets shall show great signs and wonders; behold I have told you before

schools.summary: Gill places the cry at three possible moments and takes the forewarning as notice given before the events, so that the disciples would be inexcusable if they were not on their guard; Calvin says the danger was great because men whose affairs were desperate would seek phantoms instead of Christ, and draws the sharper inference that those dismayed by predicted stumbling-blocks are inexcusable, since God is faithful and will not suffer us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

Clarke holds there would be special need of the caution about the siege, since the lower the Jews were reduced the readier they were to listen, and remarks that our Lord foretold not only the appearance of these men but the manner of their conduct; Wesley takes the saving clause as decisive, that they would deceive the elect if it were possible, but it is not possible that God should suffer the body of Christians to be so deceived.

Barnes explains the appetite for a deliverer from Rome and takes the showing of signs as pretending to miracles so nearly resembling the true as to make detection hard; Ellicott suspects the historian silence about messianic pretenders was a suppression connected with his own recognition of Vespasian, and glosses the secret chambers as a shunning of the publicity that would test their claims; Robertson separates the three words the New Testament uses of such works; Lightfoot turns to the credulity that made it possible, and how much the nation attributed to dreams.

debates.question: Is the silence of the historian about messianic pretenders a difficulty?

sides.position: yes, and it was probably a suppression of the truth connected with his own recognition of Vespasian
no; many such impostors did arise about that time, and the lower the Jews were reduced the readier they were to listen

debates.question: Can the elect be deceived?

sides.position: they would be if it were possible, but it is not possible that God should suffer the body of Christians to be so deceived
but for the warning even the Christians of Judaea might have been carried away by popular delusion

outliers: Lightfoot alone asks whether the nation was madder in its religious superstition or its taste for curious arts, and reports the fasts imposed to obtain a happy dream.
Robertson alone distinguishes the prodigy, the mighty power and the sign of God purpose, and notes that our word miracle carries only one of those notions.
themes: a cry raised by the desperate
wonders near enough to the true to deceive
a warning that removes every excuse
pretenders who avoid being tested

27.pericope_label: As the lightning cometh out of the east so shall the coming of the Son of man be; for wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together

schools.summary: Gill reaches the identification of the carcass with the Jewish people by first refusing the alternative, that it is Christ crucified, to whom the word will by no means agree; Calvin takes the proverb quite differently, as a figure of union, since by whatever methods Satan tries to scatter the children of God the sacred bond is in Christ himself, dispersion coming of departing from him in whom alone our strength lies.

Clarke alone presses the compass points as significant, finding in them the march of the Roman army from east to west, and makes the carcass the nation morally and judicially dead with the eagles the legions named for their ensigns; Wesley makes the proverb a further reason for not listening to any pretended deliverer, since the nation is already before God a dead carcass.

Barnes says the figure denotes the manner and not the quarter of the coming, rapid and unexpected, and calls the proverb one that teaches a universal truth as well as a local one; Ellicott places the reader on the dim border-land between the primary and the ultimate fulfilments, and rejects two readings of the proverb, the narrowly Roman one as too local and the fantastic one of many of the Fathers; Robertson sets the visibility of the flash against the invisibility of the false Messiahs and suggests the bird may be the griffon vulture; Lightfoot supplies the principle that the destruction of Jerusalem is frequently expressed in Scripture as though it were the destruction of the whole world.

debates.question: Does the lightning indicate direction or manner?

sides.position: manner only, rapid and unexpected, so that looking in desert or secret places is useless
direction as well, marking the march of the Roman army from east to west
visibility, in contrast to the invisibility of the false Messiahs

debates.question: What are the carcass and the eagles?

sides.position: the Jewish nation judicially dead, and the Roman legions named for their ensigns
neither that nor the patristic fancy; the Roman reading is true as far as it goes but too narrow for so wide a comparison
a figure of union rather than of judgment, the bond that keeps the children of God from being scattered

outliers: Calvin alone reads the proverb as a promise of union rather than a sentence of ruin.
Lightfoot alone states the hermeneutical principle that the fall of Jerusalem is described in Scripture as the end of a world.
themes: a coming that needs no announcing
a nation described as a corpse
birds that follow an army
one proverb read two opposite ways

29.pericope_label: Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun shall be darkened, the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven

schools.summary: Gill takes the adverb strictly, so that what follows comes to pass just upon the destruction of the city and cannot be referred to the last judgment; Calvin treats the verse as the turn to the full manifestation of the kingdom the disciples had asked about, and holds the principal object of the reply was to confirm them in good hope, which is why Christ speaks in the modes of expression common among the prophets.

Henry takes the second coming to be meant and defends the nearness of the language as the usual prophetic way of expressing the greatness and certainty of a thing, reading the whole as a great change in order to the making of all things new, and contrasting a first coming set for a sign to be spoken against with a second to be admired.

Clarke argues that the word immediately shows our Lord is not speaking of a distant event but of something consequent on calamities already predicted, and borrows the figure of a Jewish heaven whose sun and moon are the religion and government of that people; Wesley says flatly that here our Lord begins to speak of his last coming, and resolves the adverb by the speaker, since with God a thousand years are as one day.

Barnes argues from usage that the images are not literal, the sacred writers employing them for any great calamity as the fall of Babylon is foretold in just these terms; Ellicott holds that from this point the prophecy passes beyond Jerusalem to the final coming and insists no other meaning could have been found when the words were first heard; Robertson grants the adverb gives trouble if one stresses the time element, calls the passage a prophetic panorama with foreshortened perspective, and says literalism will not serve; Lightfoot supplies the figure itself, that the Jewish heaven perishes and the sun and moon of its glory are darkened.

debates.question: Does this verse describe the fall of Jerusalem or the second coming?

sides.position: the fall of Jerusalem only; the adverb forbids a distant event, and the images are the ordinary prophetic figures for a national overthrow
the final coming, the prophecy taking a wider range from this point, since no other meaning could have been found when the words were first heard
neither alternative alone; it is a prophetic panorama with foreshortened perspective, and literalism will not serve

outliers: Wesley alone explains the adverb by the speaker rather than the event, and blames a misreading of it for the primitive expectation of an immediate return.
Lightfoot alone assigns the parts of the figure, the sun to the religion of the church, the moon to the government of the state, and the stars to the judges and doctors of both.
themes: one adverb that divides the commentators
a heaven that belongs to a nation
prophetic nearness as a figure of certainty
a panorama without perspective

30.pericope_label: Then shall appear the sign of the Son of man, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn; he shall send his angels with a great trumpet to gather his elect from the four winds

schools.summary: Gill clears the ground by refusing the trumpet, the clouds and the cross in the air, his reason against the trumpet being that this sign is not said to be sounded but to appear, and makes the angels messengers rather than spirits, the ministers sent into the world of the Gentiles; Calvin uses the term to mark the difference between the present condition of Christ kingdom and its future glory, and reads the gathering from the four winds as hyperbole meant to console disciples discouraged by the Church dispersion.

Clarke makes the plain meaning a manifestation of Christ power in the destruction of the city, takes the word rendered earth to mean the land of Judaea, reads the loud trumpet as the earnest call of the gospel and the elect as the Gentiles now chosen in place of the rebellious Jews; Wesley alone ventures a guess at the sign, that it appears a little before he descends and is perhaps the cross, and defines the elect as all who have endured to the end in the faith which works by love.

Barnes allows both fulfilments at once and notes the word angels means literally messengers and is applied even to inanimate things God employs; Ellicott asks whether we can picture the sign at all and reports the wildly conjectural answers, prefers the manuscripts which omit the word sound, and admits we cannot know what reality will answer to the symbol; Robertson prefers the suggestion that Christ himself is the sign, taking the genitive as one of apposition, and holds the coming is not to be identified with the judgment of Jerusalem but forms its preternatural background; Lightfoot puts the sign as a proof of identity given in vengeance rather than in any visible figure.

debates.question: What is the sign of the Son of man?

sides.position: unknown and unpicturable; the conjectures of a cross in the sky or a dazzling flash are wild
Christ himself, the genitive being one of apposition, as the rest of the verse confirms
the destruction of the city, so signal a manifestation of his power that the tribes must mourn and own him
perhaps the cross, appearing a little before he descends

debates.question: Who are the angels and what is the trumpet?

sides.position: messengers, that is the apostles and their successors, with the trumpet the call of the gospel and the elect the Gentiles
the word can mean either messengers or the exalted intelligences, and either sense will serve here
the coming is not the judgment of Jerusalem but its preternatural background, and the trumpet is the standing prophetic signal

outliers: Ellicott alone prefers the manuscripts that omit the word sound and read simply a great trumpet.
Calvin alone turns the gathering into a consolation about the dispersion of the Church rather than a description of the last day.
themes: a sign nobody will describe
a mourning that is also an acknowledgement
messengers or angels
a gathering from the ends of the earth

32.pericope_label: Learn a parable of the fig tree; when ye see all these things know that it is near, this generation shall not pass till all these things be fulfilled, heaven and earth shall pass away but my words shall not pass away

schools.summary: Gill supplies the natural detail, that the tree was well known in Judaea and its putting forth fell under everyone observation, and alone takes the first clause about heaven and earth as an assertion about the end of time, qualifying it as true not of their substance, which will always remain, but of their qualities, so that they are renewed and refined rather than destroyed and the evil circumstances attending them through man sin pass away; Calvin refuses the obvious reading of the parable, taking it not merely that the coming will be as evident as greenness is of summer but as a comparison drawn from the greater vigour trees show after the contraction of winter, holds that Christ does not extend the discourse to all the miseries that would befall the Church but tells them they will learn his words true before a single generation is completed, and says he illustrates their certainty by making them more stable than the entire structure of the world.

Henry makes the parable the practical application of the whole prediction, that we must expect these events and prepare for them, observing the signs of the times and comparing them with the word so as to foresee what is at the door, the figure itself being no more than that budding and blossoming presage summer.

Clarke puts the parable as a proof, the signs given being as infallible evidence of the approaching ruin of the Jewish state as the budding of the trees is of the coming summer, and alone renders the disputed phrase this race, arguing that the Jews shall not cease from being a distinct people till all the counsels of God concerning them and the Gentiles are fulfilled while allowing that others translate it of the persons then living; Wesley reads the phrase as implying that a great part of that generation would be passed away but not the whole, and observes it fell out just so, the city being destroyed thirty-nine or forty years later.

Barnes makes a generation thirty or forty years and notes the destruction came about forty years after, explains that the juices return from the roots so the buds swell and burst, and puts the closing saying as a comparison, that one may sooner expect heaven and earth to return to nothing than these words to fail; Ellicott adds that the season was early spring, says the natural meaning of the disputed phrase is beyond question the one that takes it of those then living and ascribes the other rendering to a desire to bring the words into apparent harmony with history, and hears in the last verse the tone of one speaking with supreme authority, claiming for his own words the eternity belonging to the words of Jehovah; Robertson says that if the reference is to the destruction of Jerusalem there was a literal fulfilment; Lightfoot draws his inference from the phrase, that the foregoing verses cannot be of the last judgment but of the destruction of Jerusalem, since some disciples lived to see these things and some rabbis then alive survived the city fall.

debates.question: What does this generation mean?

sides.position: this race, the Jews as a distinct people, who shall not cease till all the counsels of God concerning them are fulfilled
the persons then living; the natural meaning is beyond question, and it fell out so, the city being destroyed some forty years later

debates.question: Do heaven and earth themselves pass away?

sides.position: not as to their substance, which will always remain, but as to their qualities, being renewed and refined rather than destroyed
the clause is a comparison for certainty, making his words more stable than the whole structure of the world

outliers: Clarke alone renders the phrase this race and makes the survival of the Jewish people the thing promised.
Calvin alone reads the fig tree as a figure of vigour recovered after winter rather than of a season announced by its signs.
themes: a sign as plain as a budding tree
one phrase that divides the commentators
a date fixed within forty years
words claimed to outlast the world

36.pericope_label: Of that day and hour knoweth no man, not the angels, but my Father only; as the days of Noe were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be

schools.summary: Gill restricts the unknown day, taking it not of the second coming and the last judgment but of the coming of the Son of man to take vengeance on the Jews, since the words concern the date of the things already described, and reads the days of Noah both ways, that the practices of that generation will be those of the age in which the Son of man comes and that the flood fell suddenly on men thoughtless about it although warned, who slighted Noah warnings and were given up to judicial blindness; Calvin states the purpose of the ignorance, that Christ held believers minds in suspense so that they might not by a false imagination fix any time for the final redemption, knowing how fickle our minds are and how a vain curiosity tickles us to know more than is proper, and finds the cause of the old world ignorance in unbelief, which blinded their minds where by contrast Noah beheld at a distance the vengeance still concealed and feared it early.

Clarke supports the restricted reading by translating the second noun as season rather than hour, a sense he says both sacred and profane authors use, and argues it from the earlier directions, that because the day was unknown they were to pray it might not fall on a sabbath and because the season was unknown that it might not be in winter, takes the eating and drinking to mean they spent their time in rapine, luxury and riot, and says the design of the verses is that the desolation should be as general as it was unexpected; Wesley agrees that the day of judgment is meant and adds the careful qualification that no man knew it while our Lord was on earth, though it might afterwards be revealed to John consistently with this.

Robertson takes the other side, that here Jesus has in mind his second coming, having stated plainly that the destruction of Jerusalem would happen in that generation and stating now as pointedly that no one knows this day, treats the clause about the Son as probably genuine here too, and makes the contrast sharply, that in Noah day there was plenty of warning but utter unpreparedness, as most people are now either indifferent about the second coming or have fanciful schemes about it; Ellicott fastens on the second evangelist addition, not even the Son, which he calls every way remarkable and explains by that Gospel connection with Peter, and turns the reckless apathy back on the earlier dispute, as justifying a reading of the signs of the Advent not as phenomena visible to the eye of sense but as signs of the times discerned only by the insight of the faithful; Barnes keeps to the structure of the answer, that the general signs have been given as budding indicates summer but the precise time is not indicated by them, and sets out two points of likeness to the flood, that the coming would be sudden and unexpected and that the world would be found as it was then; Lightfoot notes that Peter sets the ruin of the old world and of Jerusalem side by side as parallels.

debates.question: Which coming is the day no man knows?

sides.position: the coming in vengeance on the Jews, since the words concern the date of the things just described
the second coming and the day of judgment, stated as pointedly here as the nearness of the city fall was stated before

debates.question: In what does the likeness to the days of Noah consist?

sides.position: in unpreparedness despite ample warning, the flood falling suddenly on men who would not lay it to heart
in the manner of life, their time spent in rapine, luxury and riot
in unbelief, which blinded their minds where Noah saw the concealed vengeance from afar and feared early

outliers: Clarke alone renders the second noun season and argues the point from the earlier charge to pray against a sabbath and a winter flight.
Ellicott alone uses the apathy of the verse as evidence against taking the signs as visible to the eye of sense.
themes: a date kept in the Father own power
ignorance appointed to keep hope awake
a warned world that would not listen
signs discerned by insight rather than sight

40.pericope_label: Two in the field, one taken and one left; two women grinding at the mill; watch therefore, for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come, and had the householder known he would have watched

schools.summary: Gill observes that the word women is not in the Greek but is rightly supplied, the participle being feminine and the work belonging to women, draws the charge to watch as an inference from what precedes rather than a new subject, the time of the desolation being uncertain and coming on the Jews unawares, and makes the readiness the point rather than the figure of the thief; Calvin takes the more pointed form of the exhortation in the third Gospel, that a man whose senses are overloaded with food and wine will never raise his mind to the heavenly life, and since no desire of the flesh fails to intoxicate, they must not satiate themselves with the world.

Henry defines the watching inwardly, as maintaining the temper of mind we would be willing for our Lord to find us in, since we know we have but a little time to live and cannot know we have a long time, much less the time fixed for the judgment.

Clarke reads the pair of illustrations as a measure of how general the calamity would be, no two persons anywhere being both able to escape, captivity and the sword having a complete triumph over that unhappy people, and puts the historical result bluntly, that this advice the followers of Christ took and therefore escaped while the miserable Jews rejected it and were destroyed; Wesley takes the opposite view of the taking without hesitation, that the one is taken into God immediate protection and the other left to share the common calamities, remarks that our Lord speaks as having the whole transaction present before his eyes, and reads the uncertainty two ways at once, that the Lord may come either to require a man soul of him or to avenge himself of that nation.

Ellicott states the difficulty exactly, that the present tense expresses the certainty of the future and the form leaves it uncertain which alternative belongs to the chosen, gives the picture of the hand-mill with one woman holding the lower stone while another turns the upper and notes that elsewhere the employment appears as the crowning degradation of captives taken in battle, observes that these verses have no counterpart in the other reports but stand almost word for word in another discourse, and concludes that even the signs likened to the budding fig were meant only to rouse the faithful, not to let men fix times the Father has kept in his own power; Barnes allows both senses of the word, to be taken away from the danger and rescued or to be taken away by death, and thinks the latter probably meant, describes the stones two feet across and half a foot thick with the lower fixed and the upper turned by a handle, and puts the householder case, that a man who knew the hour would be ready; Robertson glosses the imperative as keep awake, be on the watch, notes that Jesus enforces the point with half a dozen parables that follow, prefers the reading mill to millhouse, and explains the breaking through as digging through a tile roof or under a floor of beaten earth.

debates.question: Is the one taken received or carried off?

sides.position: taken into God immediate protection, the other left to share the common calamities
probably taken away by death, though the word allows a rescue from danger
the form leaves it uncertain which alternative belongs to the chosen
the question is beside the point; the pair measures how general the calamity would be, no two persons anywhere both escaping

debates.question: What coming is the watching for?

sides.position: the desolation of Jerusalem, which came on the Jews unawares, and which the followers of Christ escaped by taking the advice
either the requiring of a man soul of him or the vengeance on that nation, both at once
a standing temper of mind, since we cannot know we have a long time to live
a sobriety against the intoxication of the flesh, which keeps the mind from rising to the heavenly life

outliers: Ellicott alone notes that these verses stand almost word for word in another discourse, so that one must choose between a repetition and a transfer.
Robertson alone explains the thief breaking through as digging through a tile roof or under a floor of beaten earth.
themes: two at the same work and one outcome
the lowest labour in the house
watchfulness as a settled temper
a householder who did not know the hour

45.pericope_label: Who then is a faithful and wise servant whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season; blessed is that servant, and his lord shall make him ruler over all his goods

schools.summary: Gill notes the Latin adds do you think and takes the question as put to the disciples to apply to themselves, observing that in the other Gospel it answers Peter question whether the exhortation was for them or for all, which makes it look particularly designed for them, allows three comings at which the servant might be found so doing, in judgment against Jerusalem, at death when his Lord removes him out of time, or at the day of judgment when the righteous judge gives him the crown, and treats the solemn preface as a guarantee, that nothing is a greater truth or more to be depended on; Calvin explains the occasion, that Christ having said the suddenness of his coming left no room for sloth, Peter asked whether the doctrine was general or belonged to the twelve alone, the disciples being always apt to think themselves unjustly treated unless given some distinction.

Clarke reads the whole as an abstract of a minister duties, holding that all should live in the same expectation of Christ coming that a servant has of his master return, having to give an exact account of the affairs left in his hands, reduces the blessedness to one thing, that it consists in his master approbation, and takes the promotion as a heavenly privilege of the faithful minister, who receives power to dispense all the blessings of the new covenant with his word accompanied by the demonstration of the Spirit, warning that much of a preacher usefulness may be lost by unfaithfulness; Wesley makes both adjectives a question to the reader, which of you aspires after this character, and defines them, wise in retaining every moment the clearest conviction that all he now has is only entrusted to him as a steward, and faithful in thinking and speaking and acting continually in a manner suitable to that conviction.

Ellicott prefers the definite article, who then is the faithful and wise servant, explains that the second word is the one ethical writers used for the moral wisdom which adapts means to ends, against the wisdom of contemplation on one side or technical skill on the other, corrects the rendering of the servant task to giving them their food rather than meat, grants that the words in their letter seem to refer only to those found watching at the final advent but says Christian insight has rightly widened them, since as there are days of the Lord in the history of churches and nations so the Lord comes to men in the crises of their own lives, and finds in the promotion an indication that the work of the faithful servant does not cease either after his removal from earthly labour or even after the final consummation of the kingdom; Barnes observes that the passage is a parable though not expressly called one, designed to show that the disciples should act as if each moment expecting their Lord return, and is careful to say what the promotion does not mean, the setting of the servant over all the property being a circumstance of the story designed to show the effect of faithfulness and not a promise that ministers shall have higher rank, the reward being God approbation.

debates.question: To whom is the question put?

sides.position: to the disciples particularly, as the answer to Peter question whether the exhortation was for them or for all
to the reader, as a question which of you aspires after this character
to all who serve, the passage being an abstract of a minister duties cast as a parable

debates.question: At what coming is the servant found so doing, and what is his reward?

sides.position: at any of three comings, in judgment against Jerusalem, at death, or at the last day, the crown being the reward
in the letter at the final advent, rightly widened by Christian insight to the crises of a man own life
the reward is his master approbation and nothing else; the promotion gives no higher rank

outliers: Ellicott alone finds in the promotion an indication that the faithful servant work continues even after the final consummation of the kingdom.
Wesley alone turns both adjectives into a challenge to the reader and defines each as a habit of mind rather than an office.
themes: a question aimed at the hearers
wisdom that fits means to ends
food given at the right time
a reward that is approbation rather than rank

48.pericope_label: But if that evil servant shall say my lord delayeth his coming and shall begin to smite his fellowservants, his lord shall come in an hour he is not aware of and shall cut him asunder and appoint him his portion with the hypocrites

schools.summary: Gill allows that such a man may have gifts and hold the highest post in the church, graceless men being sometimes in such places while destitute of the grace of God, describes the oppression in detail, the abuse of power lodged in him, the usurping of dominion over the faith of others, the imposing on consciences of what Christ never commanded, the burdening with trifling rites and the persecuting of saints who will not come into his way of believing, and offers a different reading of the sentence, the separating of soul and body by death, the taking away of his gifts and his removal from office and from the communion of saints, reporting the suggestion that the allusion is to the cutting up of sacrifices; Calvin states the matter as a diagnosis, that this is the source of the carelessness which creeps on wicked servants, that they trust to a longer delay and involve themselves in darkness of their own accord, imagining the day of account will never come and promising themselves impunity.

Clarke orders the whole passage into a scheme, finding three characters of a bad minister and three punishments to answer them, the first character being that he has little or no faith in the speedy coming of Christ, which he may not profess outwardly but says in his heart, so teaching what he does not believe, and the second that he governs with absolute dominion, oppressing his colleagues, while the punishments answer the characters, a sudden death with the weight of God judgments falling before a moment can avert it and a separation from the communion of saints and from the gifts he has abused, and he assembles the evidence for the sentence from the historians, including the report that Isaiah was sawn asunder and instances of kings who ordered men cut in two; Wesley marks the tense, that he is now evil, having put away faith and a good conscience, and presses the propriety of the word hypocrites if ministers are meant, since no hypocrisy can be baser than to call ourselves ministers of Christ while slaves of avarice, ambition or sensuality, with the prayer that God would reform them or disarm them of the influence they abuse.

Barnes glosses the clause as a secret supposition that the master will not return for a long time or perhaps not at all, makes the point briefly that the conduct is designed to represent ministers who are unfaithful and overbearing and abuse their trust in the church, says the punishment was anciently inflicted, sometimes by the sword and sometimes by saws, among the Chaldeans and Hebrews as well as the Egyptians and Romans, but holds it is perhaps not literal here and signifies only that the servant should be severely punished, and notes that the hypocrites are spoken of as the worst of offenders; Ellicott finds the temper identical with one the apostle describes and calls the words memorable as implying foreknowledge, amid words that indicate nearness, that there would be what men would take for delay, and takes the form of punishment to have been chosen for its figurative fitness rather than its literal sense, since the man had been double-minded, trying to serve two masters, and his Lord with the sharp sword of judgment smites through the false apparent unity of his life and reveals its duplicity; Robertson names the temptation that follows, to indulge fleshly appetites or the pride of superior intellect, and observes that within a generation scoffers would ask where the promise of the coming was, forgetting that God clock is not like ours.

debates.question: Is the cutting asunder literal?

sides.position: the punishment was anciently inflicted, by the sword and by saws, but is perhaps not literal here and means only severe punishment
the form was chosen for its figurative fitness, the sword of judgment smiting through the apparent unity of a double-minded life
it is the separating of soul and body by death, with the loss of his gifts and his removal from office and communion
literal enough to be documented, Isaiah reported sawn asunder and kings known to have ordered men cut in two

debates.question: Where does the evil servant fall begin?

sides.position: in a secret supposition of delay, which he trusts to and so involves himself in darkness, promising himself impunity
in having little or no faith in the speedy coming, which he does not profess outwardly but says in his heart, so teaching what he does not believe
in having put away faith and a good conscience, so that he is now evil
in gifts and office held without grace, a graceless man in the highest post in the church
in the appetites and the pride of intellect that the delay leaves room for, the temper of scoffers asking where the promise is

outliers: Clarke alone orders the passage into three characters of a bad minister with three punishments answering them one by one.
Wesley alone closes with a prayer that God would reform such ministers or disarm them of the influence they abuse.
themes: a delay assumed in the heart
authority turned against fellow servants
a sentence read as figure rather than practice
a portion appointed with the hypocrites
